question: Do you still face production defects after every release?

yes.title: Production defects are escaping release
yes.diagnosis: Production defects are still occurring after releases, indicating that the current QA process is not consistently detecting critical defects before production. This may point to gaps in test coverage, regression testing, environment parity, test data, automation, or release validation.
yes.problem: Defects escaping into production increase business risk, customer impact, rework, and cost of remediation.
recommendations: Analyze production defects by root cause.
Introduce shift-left testing.

no.title: Production defect prevention is effective
no.diagnosis: Production defects are generally being prevented before release, indicating effective quality controls and release validation.
recommendations: Continue monitoring production defect leakage and perform root-cause analysis on any escaped defects to prevent recurrence.

partial.title: Production defect prevention is inconsistent
partial.diagnosis: Production defects are reduced but still occur in certain releases, applications, or critical business areas. QA controls are working inconsistently.
recommendations: Identify where leakage is concentrated and prioritize improvements around high-risk applications, business-critical functionality, regression coverage, and automation.

question: Do your automation scripts break frequently when the application changes?

yes.title: Automation is tightly coupled to application change
yes.diagnosis: Frequent automation failures indicate that the automation framework is tightly coupled to application implementation and lacks maintainability and resilience.
yes.problem: Automation that breaks whenever the application changes creates maintenance overhead and reduces confidence in automated testing.
recommendations: Strengthen automation architecture.
Introduce self-healing capabilities.

no.title: Automation is resilient to application change
no.diagnosis: The automation suite is relatively resilient to application changes, indicating good framework architecture and maintainability.
recommendations: Continue measuring automation stability, execution reliability, maintenance effort, and business coverage.

partial.title: Automation requires significant maintenance
partial.diagnosis: Automation remains useful but requires significant maintenance when application changes occur.
recommendations: Identify weaknesses and reduce maintenance.

question: Is there enterprise tooling available and adopted consistently across QA?

yes.title: Enterprise QA tooling is standardized
yes.diagnosis: QA has standardized enterprise tooling that is consistently adopted, indicating a mature technology foundation and reduced fragmentation.
recommendations: Regularly review tooling effectiveness, utilization, integration, licensing cost, and business value.

no.title: Enterprise QA tooling is fragmented
no.diagnosis: QA teams lack consistent enterprise tooling, resulting in fragmented tools, inconsistent practices, duplicated capabilities, and potentially higher operational costs.
recommendations: Define an enterprise QA tool strategy.
Measure tool utilization and ROI.

partial.title: Enterprise tooling adoption varies
partial.diagnosis: Enterprise tooling exists, but adoption varies across teams or programs.
recommendations: Identify adoption barriers and establish common tooling standards, onboarding, governance, and adoption KPIs.

question: Have you completed your AI adoption for QA practices?

yes.title: AI adoption is established in QA
yes.diagnosis: AI capabilities have been incorporated into QA practices, indicating progress toward AI-enabled quality engineering.
recommendations: Move beyond isolated AI use cases toward measurable AI-driven productivity, autonomous testing, intelligent test generation, defect prediction, and continuous optimization.

no.title: AI adoption in QA is limited
no.diagnosis: QA has not yet sufficiently adopted AI, creating a potential productivity and scalability gap as testing becomes increasingly AI-enabled.
recommendations: Identify and prioritize high-value AI use cases across the QA lifecycle.
Explore AI agents for repetitive and time-consuming QA activities.

partial.title: AI adoption is inconsistent
partial.diagnosis: AI is being used in some QA activities, but adoption is limited, inconsistent, or experimental.
recommendations: Move from individual experimentation toward a structured AI adoption roadmap with prioritized use cases, measurable ROI, governance, and enterprise-scale adoption.

question: Are you still outsourcing your testing as T&M or fixed-price contracts rather than outcome/value-based models?

yes.title: Testing is managed as a delivery service
yes.diagnosis: Testing is primarily being consumed as a labour or project-based service rather than being managed around measurable quality outcomes.
yes.problem: T&M models can incentivize effort and resource utilization rather than productivity, automation, defect prevention, and business outcomes.
recommendations: Define outcome-based QA KPIs.
Link commercial models to measurable outcomes.

no.title: QA services are aligned to outcomes
no.diagnosis: QA services are increasingly aligned with outcomes, value, and measurable quality objectives rather than only resource consumption.
recommendations: Continue refining outcome-based KPIs and commercial models around quality, productivity, automation, and business impact.

partial.title: QA commercial models are mixed
partial.diagnosis: Some QA engagements use outcome-based models, while others still rely heavily on T&M or fixed-price arrangements.
recommendations: Identify suitable programs for transitioning to outcome-based models and establish standardized quality and productivity KPIs.

question: Do QA teams still work in silos, separate from product and delivery streams?

yes.title: QA operates in delivery silos
yes.diagnosis: QA operates separately from product and development teams, indicating a siloed quality model.
yes.problem: Quality becomes a downstream responsibility instead of a shared responsibility across the SDLC.
recommendations: Embed QA within product/delivery squads.
Integrate QA into planning and refinement.

no.title: Quality ownership is collaborative
no.diagnosis: QA operates collaboratively with product and delivery teams, indicating stronger ownership of quality across the SDLC.
recommendations: Continue expanding quality ownership into development, product management, DevOps, and business stakeholders.

partial.title: Team collaboration is inconsistent
partial.diagnosis: Some teams operate collaboratively while others remain structurally separated.
recommendations: Prioritize high-impact programs for integrated quality engineering teams and gradually establish a consistent operating model.

question: Do you lack a formal QA governance model across programs?

yes.title: Enterprise QA governance is missing
yes.diagnosis: There is no consistent enterprise-level QA governance model, resulting in inconsistent standards, metrics, processes, and quality controls.
recommendations: Define enterprise testing standards.
Establish QA governance.

no.title: QA governance is established
no.diagnosis: A formal QA governance structure exists and provides consistency across programs.
recommendations: Regularly review governance effectiveness and adapt standards to new technologies, AI adoption, DevOps, and regulatory requirements.

partial.title: QA governance is inconsistent
partial.diagnosis: Governance exists in some programs but is inconsistent across the organization.
recommendations: Create an enterprise governance framework with mandatory minimum standards while allowing program-specific flexibility.

question: Do you perform a test maturity assessment at frequent intervals?

yes.title: QA maturity is measured periodically
yes.diagnosis: The organization periodically evaluates its QA maturity, allowing it to identify capability gaps and track improvement.
recommendations: Ensure assessments produce measurable improvement roadmaps rather than becoming compliance exercises.

no.title: QA maturity is not measured regularly
no.diagnosis: The organization lacks a structured mechanism for periodically measuring QA maturity and identifying capability gaps.
recommendations: Establish periodic maturity assessments.
Define maturity dimensions and KPIs.

partial.title: QA maturity assessment is irregular
partial.diagnosis: Maturity assessments are performed, but they may be irregular, limited to certain programs, or not followed by measurable improvement actions.
recommendations: Standardize assessment frequency, scoring, ownership, and remediation tracking.

question: Do you still identify defects late in the STLC, such as during Dev, SIT, UAT, or Pre-Prod, rather than earlier in the SDLC?

yes.title: Defects are detected late
yes.diagnosis: Defects are being detected late in the delivery lifecycle, indicating insufficient shift-left quality practices.
yes.problem: Late defect detection generally increases remediation cost, delays releases, and increases delivery risk.
recommendations: Introduce early requirement reviews.
Shift testing toward unit/API/component levels.

no.title: Defects are detected early
no.diagnosis: Defects are generally detected earlier in the SDLC, indicating effective shift-left quality practices.
recommendations: Increase preventive quality engineering through automated checks, code analysis, contract testing, and AI-assisted defect prediction.

partial.title: Defect detection is partly shifted left
partial.diagnosis: Some defects are identified early, but significant defects continue to emerge during later testing stages.
recommendations: Analyze defects by lifecycle stage and focus improvement efforts on the stages where defect leakage is highest.

question: Do regression cycles still require manual effort despite automation claims?

yes.title: Regression remains heavily manual
yes.diagnosis: Regression testing still relies significantly on manual execution despite having automation capabilities, indicating insufficient automation coverage or poor automation effectiveness.
recommendations: Prioritize automation based on business risk and execution frequency.
Integrate automated regression into CI/CD pipelines for faster feedback.

no.title: Regression is largely automated
no.diagnosis: Regression testing is largely automated, reducing repetitive manual effort and improving execution speed.
recommendations: Optimize regression suites using risk-based selection, parallel execution, and intelligent test prioritization.

partial.title: Regression automation is incomplete
partial.diagnosis: Some regression areas are automated, but significant manual regression remains.
recommendations: Prioritize high-frequency and high-risk manual scenarios for automation and continuously retire redundant tests.

question: Do you have a test strategy documented and followed?

yes.title: The test strategy is established
yes.diagnosis: A documented test strategy exists and is actively followed, indicating structured and repeatable QA practices.
recommendations: Review the strategy periodically and align it with automation, DevOps, AI, risk-based testing, and business objectives.

no.title: A consistent test strategy is missing
no.diagnosis: QA activities are not governed by a consistent documented test strategy, increasing the risk of inconsistent coverage and execution.
recommendations: Create an enterprise/program-level test strategy.
Define appropriate test levels, types, and approaches across the SDLC.

partial.title: The test strategy is not consistently followed
partial.diagnosis: A test strategy exists but is not consistently followed or updated across programs.
recommendations: Establish ownership, governance, review cycles, and compliance mechanisms for the strategy.

yes.title: UAT relies heavily on manual execution
yes.diagnosis: UAT relies heavily on manual execution, indicating an opportunity to improve business validation efficiency and repeatability.
yes.problem: Business acceptance often requires human judgment. The maturity gap is excessive manual execution of repeatable validation, not the presence of human judgment.
recommendations: Automate repeatable UAT scenarios.
Introduce business-readable automated tests.

no.title: UAT uses efficient validation mechanisms
no.diagnosis: UAT is supported by automation or other efficient validation mechanisms, reducing repetitive manual business testing.
recommendations: Increase automated coverage of repeatable acceptance scenarios while retaining human validation for business judgment.

partial.title: UAT automation is incomplete
partial.diagnosis: Some UAT scenarios are automated, but significant repeatable validation remains manual.
recommendations: Categorize UAT scenarios into automatable and human-judgment scenarios and progressively automate the repeatable portion.

question: Do you measure your team productivity and year-on-year productivity gain?

yes.title: QA productivity is measured
yes.diagnosis: The organization measures QA productivity and tracks improvement over time, enabling data-driven workforce and transformation decisions.
recommendations: Align productivity measures with quality outcomes and transformation decisions.

no.title: QA productivity is not measured systematically
no.diagnosis: QA productivity is not systematically measured, making it difficult to quantify efficiency improvements or demonstrate transformation value.
recommendations: Establish a balanced productivity framework combining effort, speed, quality, automation, and business outcomes.

Measure productivity alongside quality using metrics such as test execution efficiency, automation leverage, defect prevention, defect leakage, cycle time, AI-assisted productivity, and cost per quality outcome.

partial.title: Productivity measurement is incomplete
partial.diagnosis: Some productivity metrics exist, but year-on-year improvement is not consistently measured or connected to business outcomes.
recommendations: Create standardized productivity KPIs and establish a baseline against which future improvements can be measured.

question: Do you have a competency development plan for each resource?

yes.title: Individual competency development is planned
yes.diagnosis: Individual competency development is planned, indicating that the organization actively manages capability growth.
recommendations: Align competency plans with emerging QA capabilities such as automation engineering, cloud, DevOps, data testing, AI, and quality engineering.

no.title: Individual competency plans are missing
no.diagnosis: There is no structured individual competency development plan, creating a risk of skill stagnation and capability gaps.
recommendations: Establish role-based skill and competency matrices.
Provide opportunities for hands-on application through projects, POCs, and real-world assignments.

partial.title: Competency planning is inconsistent
partial.diagnosis: Development plans exist for some employees but are not consistently maintained across the QA organization.
recommendations: Standardize competency assessment and development planning across all QA resources.

question: Is your entire testing still happening by people instead of AI agents?

yes.title: Testing relies almost entirely on people
yes.diagnosis: QA activities rely almost entirely on human execution, indicating limited adoption of AI-enabled quality engineering.
yes.problem: The objective is human plus AI augmentation: AI agents handle repetitive, scalable activities and humans handle judgment, risk, strategy, and governance.
recommendations: Identify repetitive QA activities suitable for AI.
Introduce AI agents for selected autonomous workflows.

no.title: AI is augmenting the testing lifecycle
no.diagnosis: AI is already augmenting or automating part of the testing lifecycle, indicating progress toward AI-enabled QA.
recommendations: Expand AI adoption into higher-value activities while maintaining governance, traceability, security, and human oversight.

partial.title: AI augmentation is limited
partial.diagnosis: AI is being used for selected QA activities, but most testing still depends on conventional human-driven processes.
recommendations: Identify the highest-volume repetitive activities and progressively introduce AI augmentation with measurable productivity and quality targets.

question: Do you have an investment plan for continuous QA training and upskilling?

yes.title: Continuous QA capability development is funded
yes.diagnosis: The organization actively invests in continuous QA capability development, supporting long-term transformation and workforce readiness.
recommendations: Tie training investments to strategic capability gaps and measure whether training results in actual improvements in productivity, quality, automation, and technology adoption.

no.title: Continuous QA capability investment is missing
no.diagnosis: There is no structured investment plan for continuous QA capability development, increasing the risk of skill gaps as technology and testing practices evolve.
recommendations: Establish an annual QA capability development roadmap.
Allocate a dedicated training and upskilling budget.

partial.title: Training investment is inconsistent
partial.diagnosis: Training occurs, but investment is inconsistent, reactive, or not aligned with a defined capability strategy.
recommendations: Create a structured annual capability plan with defined budget, skill priorities, learning paths, and measurable outcomes.
